content: Women with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) who undergo surgical treatment may face an increased risk of infertility. Specifically, restorative proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) has been associated with a potential rise in infertility, though the exact extent of this risk remains unclear. The effects of other types of IBD-related surgeries on infertility are not well understood. The primary aim of this research was to assess how surgical interventions for IBD impact female infertility. Secondary objectives included evaluating the influence of these surgeries on assisted reproductive technology (ART) use, time to conception, miscarriage rates, stillbirths, preterm births, delivery methods (vaginal, instrumental, or Caesarean), neonatal outcomes (such as resuscitation needs, neonatal intensive care unit admission, low birth weight, and small for gestational age), and maternal complications (including gestational diabetes, hypertension, preeclampsia, postpartum depression, and hemorrhage). A comprehensive search of databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and others, was conducted up to September 27, 2018, to identify relevant studies. Observational studies involving women of reproductive age (≥12 years) with IBD who underwent surgery were included. Comparisons were made between women who had surgery and those who did not, as well as between preand post-surgical states. Infertility was defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of unprotected intercourse, with additional assessments at 6, 18, and 24 months. Studies involving women without IBD or comparing women with IBD to those without IBD were excluded. Sixteen observational studies were included, with ten contributing to meta-analyses. Among these, nine studies compared women with and without prior IBD-related surgery, while one compared open versus laparoscopic IPAA. Four studies specifically evaluated infertility, one examined ART use, and seven reported on pregnancy-related outcomes. Seven additional studies compared women before and after colectomy and/or IPAA, with five focusing on infertility, three on ART use, and three on other pregnancy-related outcomes. All studies were found to have a high risk of bias in at least two domains. The evidence regarding the impact of IBD surgery on infertility at 12 months (RR 5.45, 95% CI 0.41 to 72.57; 114 participants; 2 studies) and 24 months (RR 3.59, 95% CI 1.32 to 9.73; 190 participants; 1 study) is highly uncertain. Women who underwent laparoscopic surgery appeared to have lower infertility rates at 12 months compared to those who had open restorative proctocolectomy (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.27; 37 participants; 1 study). However, the evidence remains inconclusive. Regarding pregnancy-related outcomes, women with prior IBD surgery showed higher odds of miscarriage (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.14 to 3.60; 776 pregnancies; 5 studies), increased use of ART (RR 25.09, 95% CI 1.56 to 403.76; 106 participants; 1 study), and a greater likelihood of Caesarean section delivery (RR 2.23, 95% CI 1.00 to 4.95; 20 pregnancies; 1 study). The risks of stillbirth (RR 1.96, 95% CI 0.42 to 9.18; 246 pregnancies; 3 studies), preterm birth (RR 1.91, 95% CI 0.67 to 5.48; 194 pregnancies; 3 studies), low birth weight (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.08 to 4.83), and small for gestational age infants (RR 2.54, 95% CI 0.80 to 8.01; 65 pregnancies; 1 study) were also evaluated, but the findings were inconclusive due to poor-quality evidence. When comparing preand post-surgical states, infertility rates were numerically higher after surgery at 6 months (20.0% before vs. 60.0% after; 1 study), 12 months (20.8% before vs. 63.4% after; 5 studies), and 24 months (15.7% before vs. 70.1% after; 2 studies). ART use also increased after surgery, ranging from 30.3% to 34.3% compared to 5.3% to 42.2% before surgery. Caesarean section rates were higher post-surgery (11.0% before vs. 48.0% after; 2 studies). Time to conception was longer after surgery (2–5 months post-surgery vs. 5–16 months pre-surgery; 2 studies). Miscarriage (15.4% before vs. 15.7% after; 3 studies) and stillbirth rates (5.3% before vs. 3.8% after; 2 studies) were similar before and after surgery. Gestational diabetes was less common after surgery (8.1% before vs. 0% after; 1 study), while preeclampsia rates were comparable (5.4% before vs. 0% after; 1 study). Overall, the quality of evidence was rated as very low due to the observational nature of the studies, small sample sizes, imprecise estimates, and high risk of bias. The findings suggest that IBD-related surgery may increase the risk of infertility and adverse pregnancy outcomes, but the evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions. Further well-designed studies are needed to clarify the impact of surgical interventions on female fertility and pregnancy outcomes.
